title: Frog Jump II
summary: Given a 0-indexed integer array stones sorted in strictly increasing order, representing the positions of stones in a river, a frog starts at the first stone and aims to reach the last stone before returning to the first stone.
statement: Given a 0-indexed integer array stones sorted in strictly increasing order, representing the positions of stones in a river, a frog starts at the first stone and aims to reach the last stone before returning to the first stone. The frog can make at most one jump to any stone. The length of a jump is the absolute difference between the positions of the stones the frog is currently on and the stone it jumps to. The cost of a path is defined as the maximum length of a jump in the path. Determine the minimum cost for the frog to complete its journey.
constraints: Stone positions are strictly increasing; the frog travels from the first to last and returns.
Every intermediate stone may be visited at most once across the round trip.
Minimize the largest single jump length.
hints: An optimal trip alternates intermediate stones between outbound and return paths.
Each pair of stones two indexes apart must be connected on at least one direction, giving a lower bound on their gap.
Take the maximum two-apart gap, including the first adjacent gap.
Alternating stones realizes exactly those jumps, so the unavoidable lower bound is achievable.
editorial: Alternating stones realizes exactly those jumps, so the unavoidable lower bound is achievable.

tests.explanation: Alternating intermediate stones between the two directions gives a minimum possible largest jump of five.
The middle stone can serve only one direction, so the other direction jumps directly from zero to nine.
